# AxiomDynamics — Current State

**Last updated:** 2026-11-13 (**chat-9 closed**). Next session: read
`CURRENT-STATE.md`, then `project-logs/chat-9/CARRY-FORWARD.md`. Suite **370**,
mutation driver **24 mutations, 24 killed**. Chat-9 closed item 1's last
software half: **a disposition cannot exist without an attestation**.
Account: `assets/attestation-at-entry-build-2026-11-13.md`.

**The buildable queue inside this repository is near-empty.** Three of chat-9's
six rungs are blocked outside it: the real payload schema needs the Railroad, the
supply-chain application needs a release host and a GPG key with custody, and
D07 §14.5 needs counsel. Chat-10 should start by re-deriving the ladder rather
than assuming there is code to write.
**Repository:** `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics`
**Remote:** `github.com/kaanju19-lang/AxiomDynamics` (private)
**Push state:** `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD` is the only answer that
counts. As last confirmed the local remote-tracking ref stood at `bb99cdd`; the
first commit after it is `893096e`. Never trust a hash written in this file
— check with git, because this file's own commit moves the top of the branch
every time it is edited. Run `PUSH-TO-GITHUB.bat` in the repo root. The sandbox
cannot reach GitHub: `git push` and `git fetch` both fail with HTTP 403 from the
proxy, so a local `origin/main` ref is not proof of what the remote holds.

---

## Chat-6 build — authenticated disposition entry (AD-2 entry half), 2026-11-11

**Built and committed in chat-6: commits `db569a4` and `83010d0`. Suite
238 → 315, all green. Not yet pushed.** Full account:
`assets/session-entry-build-2026-11-11.md`.

The gap chat-5 left: `POST /api/warrant/<id>/disposition` read `reviewer_name`
and `cert_id` out of the request body, so the name on a decision was a claim even
though the registry could verify one after the fact. `backend/accounts.py` now
binds an account to a live certification record and gates entry on a bearer
token; identity comes from the resolved session and a body carrying either field
is **refused**. `resolve_session` re-checks the certificate, and a second check
runs inside the ledger's write transaction so a revocation landing between
resolve and INSERT cannot record a decision. With no account enrolled the path is
**closed (503)** rather than reopened to free text. `tools/seed_demo_account.py`
is the deliberate act that opens it. The frontend now signs in; the reviewer and
certification boxes are gone because they would be a lie about what the row says.

**The audit is the part worth reading.** An independent agent told to *falsify*
the claim found the transaction guard **inert** — it *returned* a boolean and the
caller discarded it, so a certificate revoked in the resolve-to-INSERT window
still produced HTTP 200 and a row. 310 tests were green. They missed it because
the test simulated the race with a guard that *raised*, which is not the guard
the route installs. A guard whose only tested failure mode is one the caller does
not use is not a guard — the same shape as the vacuous ledger and ROI tests.
Fixed, with the exploit reproduced verbatim against the fix's removal.

Also fixed from the hostile-input sweep: two 500s on malformed bodies
(`note` as an object, `disposition` as a list).

Still open: **key custody and joiner/mover/leaver** (a written procedure), a
**signed key directory**, and requiring an **attestation** at entry as well as a
session. Entry proves a credential was presented; it does not prove a person.

## Chat-8 phase one — the four mutation survivors are closed, 2026-11-11

Commit `a4ccc0b`. **Driver: 18 mutations, 18 killed, 0 survived. Suite 346 → 351.**
Account: `assets/mutation-survivors-closed-2026-11-11.md`.

M5 and M9 were the straightforward coverage gaps the carry-forward described.
M3 needed a case nothing had: a garbage body **plus an unknown token** — with
the resolve failure swallowed, that is the one shape where a row reaches the
ingest log while the status stays 401. **M2 was not the gap it was reported to
be**; I first decided it was an equivalent mutant and was wrong, because the
status and the row count match but the **error text does not**. The test now
asserts the message.

**Two defects in the driver itself were found by an independent audit after
every mutation was green**, and both matter more than the tests:

- An `EQUIVALENT` table I added was keyed by mutation **index**. The auditor
  put a genuine survivor in that slot and the driver printed "equivalent" and
  exited **0**. It would have absorbed any real survivor landing there.
  Removed; a survivor now always prints `ALIVE`.
- The pycache isolation was **inert**: the suite runs under `-I`, and `-I`
  sets `sys.pycache_prefix` to `None`, discarding `PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX`.
  Bytecode still reached the source tree. Now `-X pycache_prefix=...`, which
  `-I` honours — both claims verified rather than assumed.

**Importing `backend.main` runs `store.init_db()`** against the repo root, so a
test that imports it before setting `AXIOM_DB_PATH` creates an `axiom.db` there
and dies with `disk I/O error` on this mount. `tests/test_ingest_auth.py` now
sets it first.

**`project-logs/close-gate.sh` carries chat-7's session path** and will fail
from any other session. Fix its paths before chat-8 closes.

## Chat-8 phase two — the AD-2 custody procedure, 2026-11-11

Commit `3de44cf`. B01 §7 item 1 has been open on "key custody and
joiner/mover/leaver — a written procedure, not code" since chat-6. It is now
**D09 §8.4**, eight subsections, beside §4.5 which already does the same job for
the export key. Account: `assets/key-custody-procedure-2026-11-11.md`.
**Suite 351 → 359.**

**Writing the procedure down exposed three things the code did not support, and
no test found any of them.** That is the part worth carrying:

- **A key could be registered to a second reviewer, and the second one won.**
  `register` refused only a key revoked *anywhere* in its history; a *live* key
  presented under a different reviewer was accepted, and because `attest`
  resolves the newest entry for a `key_id` — deliberately, so renewal works —
  the second reviewer took the key over and the original holder was locked out
  of their own key. The register is append-only, so the binding could never be
  removed. Now refused at the write. A renewal under a new certificate for the
  **same** reviewer still works; my first attempt refused that too and would
  have broken rotation to fix sharing.
- **A refused key directory still handed back bindings** — `ok=False` alongside
  `bindings={'<key>': 'Hoffman'}` for the directory it had just refused. Now
  `{}`.
- **The procedure named a step nobody could perform.** The only code that made
  a reviewer key was `seed_demo_account.py`, which generates one and discards
  it. `tools/issue_reviewer_key.py` is the joiner step: generate, register,
  print the `key_id`, never the key, refuse to overwrite an existing key file.

Every mechanism claim in §8.4 was executed rather than reasoned about. Both new
guards are mutation-tested — each fails exactly one test when removed.
**Item 1 is not closed:** a credential holder is not a person, the HMAC scheme
is symmetric, a demo cannot attest, and every step but revocation is performed
by a human. What changed is that the item is now auditable under D09 §10.1, and
B01 §7 item 1 says that rather than implying a document settles it.

## Chat-9 — attestation at entry, and a generator defect four chats old, 2026-11-13

Commits `0916bc0`, `e2bdf6d`, `fec966b`. **Suite 359 → 370.** Three rungs landed
and three are blocked outside the repository.

**Attestation at entry closes B01 §7 item 1's last software half.** A disposition
now requires the session token **and** a registered reviewer key, and the
attestation is written **inside the ledger's own transaction** — so a refused key
rolls the whole write back and no row can exist that no key vouched for. The
design was forced, not chosen: the registry stores only the 16-hex `key_id`, an
attestation is an HMAC the server must compute, and it covers `recorded_at`,
`prev_hash` and `supersedes_id`, none of which exist until the row is built. The
key is therefore presented per request in `X-Reviewer-Key`. Making it the login
credential was rejected because it would put the attestation secret in the
session store and its backups. **Item 1 is still open** — a credential holder is
not a person — and B01 says so in its own words.

**Two defects this exposed, both mine.** `seed_demo_account.py` generated the
reviewer key and discarded it, so after the change a seeded operator could sign
in and have every write refused — the same "procedure naming a step nobody can
perform" shape as chat-8. `--key-file` now writes it 0600.

And **three of six mutations survived the first run**, all three because the
assertion matched the wrong message: `"reviewer key"` also appears in the
*unregistered-key* message, the inner guard also names both reviewers, and every
route test was refused at the **early** check so the transactional layer was
never reached. **Two layers of one check cannot both be tested through the outer
layer.** Three direct `save_disposition` tests now reach the inner guard; all 24
mutations are killed.

**A generator defect four rebuilds old was found in the same pass.**
`inlineRuns()` and `PB()` both handled bold and code and **neither handled
single-asterisk italics**, so fifteen italic phrases rendered literally —
including in stages written four chats ago. It hid because there were two
near-identical tokenisers and the one with the gap was not the one every
paragraph used. Now a single `tokenize()`.

**Three documents still said entry was ungated** (D00's F08 row, D09 §4.4, F09
Part 7) after chat-6 closed that gap. Corrected; `close-gate.sh` greps for the
phrasing so the next one trips the gate.

## What this project is

Physics-first predictive maintenance for freight rail. Six named physical models
— thermodynamics with per-axle rolling z-score, peer median/MAD comparison,
kinematics, acoustics (BPFO/BPFI/BSF/FTF), same-axle left/right differential, and
an executive ROI panel — instead of black-box ML or fixed alarm thresholds.

The Master Brief Docket is in `client-assets/MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/`: 38 artifacts
— 36 Markdown documents, the A1 Excel model (with its build script beside it) and
the B03 HTML infographic — across A (commercial), B (technical), C (deployment)
and D (contractual) series plus F (forms).

## Build status

**38 artifacts on disk; 37 docket IDs on disk (A1 is a folder holding the `.xlsx`
and the builder, so it counts as one ID and two files).** The docket index (D00)
carries 37 ID rows; 34 are marked `**Built**` in bold, and B02 (.md) and B03
(.html) carry plain "Built" with a format qualifier. D00 Part IV is the authority
on status, not this file.

A long-form account of the whole build — every stage, every document, every
correction, and the loss and rebuild — is at
`project-logs/AxiomDynamics-Build-History-and-Working-Summary.docx` (39 pages,
revised 2026-11-11 to carry chat-6). It is generated by
`project-logs/build-history-summary.js`; re-run
`node project-logs/build-history-summary.js` after a material change.

Open docket items are tracked in **D00 Part IV** — that table is the authority,
not this file.

## The largest known gap

**The ingest chain is built; nothing downstream is wired to it.** As of
2026-11-11 `POST /api/ingest` accepts a payload and applies schema → timestamp →
plausibility in that order: accepted for scoring (202), retained as suspect
without scoring (200), or refused with a named reason and logged (422). 24
tests. No outcome other than `accepted` emits an advisory.

Three parts remain open, disclosed in B01 §7 item 5 and B02 §2: the payload
schema is a **demonstration schema** (`axiom-detector-payload/v1`) and the real one
must be agreed with the Railroad; **the endpoint has no authentication**, which
makes it a data-poisoning route until AD-2 lands and is why it belongs on a
trusted segment; and **the demonstration fleet still scores synthetic traces** —
an accepted payload is validated and logged, not scored.

Every demonstration number therefore still demonstrates **the method**, not the
Railroad's data.

## Open items, in priority order

1. **D07 §14.5 — governing law and venue.** An open counsel decision, correctly
   labelled as open as of chat-2 (previously a blank pointing at an Order field
   that does not exist). Must be closed by signed addendum before first execution.
2. **Session-bound disposition entry, export-key identity and off-box carriage**
   — the signed export landed 2026-11-09, the **series build landed 2026-11-10**,
   and **per-disposition attribution landed 2026-11-11**
   (`backend/attribution.py`: append-only,
   **hash-chained** reviewer registry, HMAC attestations over each row's
   `record_hash` carried inside exported records, checked by both verifiers).
   What that closes: a bundle can now say which *registered reviewer key*
   attested a row, and a recipient can verify it. What remains: the *export*
   signature is still symmetric, so a bundle names no export signer;
   attribution is about a key holder, not a person, and a recipient given no
   reviewer key cannot tell an honest attestation from a fabricated one; entry
   is now gated on a **live session** but not on an attestation, so an attested
   row is still the reviewer's choice; nothing proves when a bundle was made; a ledger wiped
   before the first bundle in a series stays invisible; and **nothing carries
   the produced series off the box** — deliberate, because D09 §3.2 promises no
   outbound network, so carriage is the Railroad's physical step under §3.3.
   D09 §4.4–4.5, B01 §4.5a and §7 items 1 and 11–12. **Attribution and
   session-bound entry are no longer AD-2 dependencies; export-key identity,
   key custody and joiner/mover/leaver still are.**
   An independent adversarial audit found nine defects in this build after the
   suite was green — the worst of them let a registered key relabel another
   reviewer's row and pass both verifiers. 40 mutations, 40 killed. See
   `assets/attribution-build-2026-11-11.md`.
3. **D09 §4.4 supply-chain gaps** — SBOM (Q1 2027), hash verification of
   dependency downloads (Q1 2027), GPG-signed releases (Q2 2027). All three now
   have **tools built 2026-11-11**; none is **applied**, and D09 §4.4 carries the
   three-state distinction per control.

## Model decision — A1 governs, decided 2026-11-10 (chat-4)

The owner delegated the choice ("you decide"). **A1 governs the commercial
numbers, expressed as Option D in `assets/a2-d08-model-decision-2026-11-09.md`**:
0.05% escalation probability, $500,000 typical contained cost, $1.0B catastrophic.

What changed in the docket, all on 2026-11-10:

- **A2 §3.2 and D08 §3** anchors restated from the withdrawn 2.0x/4.1x to
  **1.77x at 500 axles, 3.36x at 10,000**, with the cost basis stated in the text
  instead of left to inference. The pilot year is charged in full and credited with
  no benefit in that calculation — the conservative frame.
- **D08 §5 restated** from A1: pilot year at the **200 axles §2 actually scopes**
  ($278,670 modelled benefit, **0.75x** the $370,000 fee — the pilot does not pay
  for itself and the document now says so); production years at 500 axles
  ($696,675/yr); four-year return **2.01x**.
- **D08 §6 restated**: six-year return **2.06x**. Close to flat against the
  four-year figure, because fee escalation from Year 4 offsets the dilution of one
  weak pilot year across more production years. It does **not** fall.
- **`backend/roi.py`** corrected: `P_CATASTROPHIC_GIVEN_MISSED_DEFECT` 2% → 0.05%,
  and the per-missed-defect value now blends the **$500,000 typical** cost rather
  than the $9.25M midpoint of the two NTSB severe benchmarks. Expected cost per
  missed defect is now **$999,750**, identical to A1's B22; the 29x overstatement is
  gone. The severe benchmarks survive as `SEVERE_FAILURE_COST_*`, explicitly
  reference-only, and the dataclass field renamed `severe_cost_range_usd` so no
  reader mistakes them for the typical case again.
- Checkers updated rather than left certifying stale text: the arithmetic pass is
  now **89 checks** and reports both findings **closed and checked**, not merely
  recorded. The decision paper's **65 checks** still reproduce (it documents the
  withdrawn figures, which is its job).

**Two things a future reader will otherwise trip over.** First, A2 §3.2 says 1.77x
at 500 axles and D08 §5 says 2.01x — different questions on the same inputs (A2
charges the pilot with no benefit; D08 credits the 200-axle pilot with its actual
benefit). A2 §3.2 now states that difference explicitly. Second, **D08 §2 scopes the
pilot at 100–200 axles**, so any pilot-year benefit computed at 500 was contradicting
the document's own scope. That defect was mine, introduced in the first restatement
and caught before commit.

## Ledger replication series — built 2026-11-10 (chat-4)

`backend/ledger_replication.py` executes the cadence D09 §4.5.4 already
specified: monthly full, weekly incremental, every bundle chained to the
previous by `previous_export_hash`, zero-record weeks kept, nothing overwritten.
`inspect` opens every bundle, recomputes its digest, verifies it against the
predecessor, and reports a missing period. 32 tests; full suite **112**.

**It deliberately does not transmit.** D09 §3.2 promises the Platform has no
outbound network, so the series accumulates in `--series-dir` on the box and
carrying it to backup media is the Railroad's step under §3.3. The owner chose
this over a network push on 2026-11-10; the reasoning is in
`assets/ledger-replication-build-2026-11-10.md`.

**Two audits found nine material defects before this was called built** — the
count is in the assets file rather than here, but the shape is worth carrying:
the release verifier rejected every full export, `inspect` could not see
tampering or gaps, the period walker hung on a 53-week ISO year, concurrent runs

== B01 §7 rows ==
140:| 1 | Reviewer authentication | **Partly built 2026-11-11.** `backend/attribution.py` implements the certification registry: per-reviewer 32-byte keys, an append-only hash-chained registry with `BEFORE UPDATE`/`BEFORE DELETE`/`BEFORE INSERT … OR REPLACE` triggers, and HMAC attestations over each row's `record_hash` that travel inside exported records. `attest()` refuses an unregistered key, a revoked key, a key registered to a different reviewer, and a key registered under a different certificate; `register()` refuses a key revoked anywhere in its history, **and — since 2026-11-11 — a live key presented under a second reviewer**, which it previously accepted, silently transferring the key and locking its original holder out of attesting. A renewed certificate for the same reviewer may still reuse the key. Both verifiers check reviewer, certificate, registration-before-attestation and revocation-on-time, and recompute the attestation when the reviewer's key is supplied **together with the name bound to it** — a key alone cannot establish the label, because the HMAC covers the row hash and not the name. The registry is **hash-chained, not signed**: it is tamper-evident to a reader who recomputes the chain, which is weaker than authentication and is described that way everywhere it appears. **Entry is now gated 2026-11-11.** `backend/accounts.py` binds an account to a live certification record already in the registry, stores a PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 verifier (600,000 iterations, per-account salt) rather than a passphrase, and issues a bearer token of which only the SHA-256 digest is stored. `POST /api/warrant/<id>/disposition` requires that token: reviewer name and certificate ID are taken from the resolved session and **never from the request body**, and a body carrying either field is refused rather than ignored. `resolve_session` re-checks that the session is unrevoked and unexpired, that the account is live, **and that the certification behind it is still live**, so a certificate revoked mid-session stops writing immediately; a second check runs inside the ledger's own write transaction, closing the resolve-to-INSERT window. With no account enrolled the path is **closed**, not opened back up to free text. The account register is append-only and hash-chained over salt, iteration count and verifier — a swap of any of the three would hand over the account. **Established by an independent audit told to falsify it**, which found the transaction guard inert because it returned a boolean and the caller discarded it; fixed, with the exploit reproduced verbatim against the fix's removal. What this still does not do is prove a human was at the keyboard, protect the token in transit (§7 item 10), or make attestation stronger — and entry now requires an attestation as well as a live session (2026-11-11): the caller must present a registered reviewer key, it is checked against the session's reviewer and certificate, and the attestation is written inside the ledger's own transaction so a refused key leaves no row | AD-2 remainder: **key custody and joiner/mover/leaver procedure** — a written process, **now written in D09 §8.4**, with issuance in `tools/issue_reviewer_key.py`. **The signed key directory is built 2026-11-11:** `backend/key_directory.py` publishes a signed list of reviewer↔key_id↔cert_id bindings (no key material), `tools/publish_key_directory.py` builds it on the Platform host and refuses if the registry chain does not verify, and `tools/verify_key_directory.py` verifies it on a recipient machine importing nothing from `backend/`. It **proves the export-key holder authored those bindings, not that they are entitled to** — the signature is symmetric — so it is portable and tamper-evident rather than authenticated. Attestation is required at entry since 2026-11-11 |
141:| 2 | Ledger append-only | **Corrected 2026-11-09, hardened 2026-11-11.** Insert-only write path; `supersedes_id` for corrections; `BEFORE UPDATE`/`BEFORE DELETE` triggers abort, plus `BEFORE INSERT ... WHEN EXISTS` refusing `INSERT OR REPLACE` over an existing id; SHA-256 chain across rows | Built — superseded decisions retained, chain verified on demand |
142:| 3 | Timestamps | SQLite `datetime('now')` default | Server-generated with NTP-synced clock |
143:| 4 | Storage durability | The demonstration environment's storage is ephemeral — the demo database is lost on spin-down | Persistent volume on Railroad hardware |
144:| 5 | Sensor ingest | **The validation chain and collector authentication are built 2026-11-11; the payload schema is not the Railroad's.** `backend/ingest.py` implements B02 §2's three gates (schema → timestamp → plausibility) over a versioned demonstration schema, fails closed, and logs every outcome. **Ingest is now authenticated 2026-11-11.** `backend/ingest_auth.py` gives a collector its own credential, deliberately separate from a reviewer account: a collector is enrolled by name, receives a 32-byte bearer token once (only the SHA-256 digest is stored), and the registry is append-only and hash-chained. `POST /api/ingest` checks the credential **before reading or logging the body** — an earlier draft logged unparseable bodies on the way in, so any anonymous caller could append rows to the ingest log; the gate now runs first, and a missing, dead or unissued token is a 401 while a deployment with no enrolled collector is **closed (503)** rather than reopened to anonymous traffic. A collector token has **no TTL and is not invalidated by revoking its enrollment**, because a collector is scheduled software rather than a person who has left; revoking stops new tokens being issued. **A Railroad payload is accepted, validated and logged — but the demonstration fleet still generates its signals from physics equations on synthetic traces, so no number in the demo moves because of ingested data.** | Real detector payload schema, defined and versioned with the Railroad |
145:| 6 | Time source | Host clock, unsynchronized | NTP to Railroad-approved source |
146:| 7 | Update mechanism | **Partly addressed 2026-11-11.** Deploys are still via git, but a release can now be built reproducibly and signed: `tools/sign_release.py` writes a deterministic archive plus the `MANIFEST.sha256` C01 Part C2 expects, signs it with a detached GPG signature, and verifies against a supplied public key. The release path installs with `--require-hashes`. **What is missing is organisational, not code:** a GPG key must be generated, its custody written, its public half published by a route the Railroad trusts, and `requirements.txt` pinned on a host with index access (`tools/pin_requirements.py`) — until that last step the Docker build **fails by design** rather than installing unpinned | Offline signed update packages with a published key, see D06 and D09 §7.3 |
147:| 8 | Audit export | **Corrected 2026-11-09, hardened 2026-11-10 and 2026-11-11.** Signed HMAC-SHA256 bundle written by `backend/ledger_export.py`; verified by `tools/verify_ledger_export.py`, which imports nothing from the Platform. Bundles chain via `previous_export_hash` and carry the ledger head so truncation is detectable against a held bundle. Verification requires the bundle to be exactly the four signed parts — an added top-level field is rejected with `bundle_no_extras`, and duplicate JSON keys are refused outright. **2026-11-11: `history_continues` now catches a rewritten history against a held bundle, which `no_truncation` alone did not.** 48 adversarial tests | Built — but see the trust-anchor item below, and read §4.5a on the one-record scope of `history_continues` |
148:| 9 | Repo hygiene | `axiom.db` and `__pycache__` were committed | Corrected; `.gitignore` added |
149:| 10 | TLS on the box | Plain HTTP | TLS or network isolation; Railroad's internal standard |
150:| 11 | **Export signing key provenance** | The key is an operator-held 32-byte secret with a printed `key_id`; its authenticity rests on a written custody procedure, not on a signature from a trusted issuer. The signature is symmetric, so any verifier can also forge | AD-2: bind the key to an issued certification record, or replace HMAC with an asymmetric signature and a published public key |
151:| 12 | **Off-box replication** | **Partly closed 2026-11-10.** `backend/ledger_replication.py` now produces the D09 §4.5.4 series on a cadence — monthly full, weekly incremental, each bundle chained to the previous by `previous_export_hash`, zero-record weeks kept, nothing overwritten — and its `inspect` verifies each bundle against the one before it and flags a missing period. What it does **not** do is move anything off the box, deliberately: D09 §3.2 promises the Platform has no outbound network, so carrying the series away is the Railroad's physical step under §3.3. Until that step happens a lost disk still loses the ledger, and a missed run is *visible* in the series rather than prevented by it | Scheduled export to a second host, with the receipt acknowledged per D09 §4.4 |

7:**The principle behind this docket:** one service, one set of terms, no parallel side-letters. Every document in here must reconcile with every other. Where two documents could conflict, **the precedence ladder in Part IV of this document governs** — D02 contains no precedence clause of its own, and an index that points at a clause that does not exist is the same dangling-reference failure it exists to prevent. This exists to close the single most common loophole in rail technology contracts: a technical annex that promises something the master agreement disclaims.
165:**Status: CLOSED** — B05 verified against code: zero outbound calls. D09 §3.2 and D07 §7.1 both state it contractually. The supply-chain controls (dependency pinning, hash verification, SBOM and signed release artefacts) are built as of 2026-11-11 and their **applied** state — a pinned file, a shipped SBOM, an issued key — is tracked in D09 §4.4 and Part VI below rather than papered over.
203:## Part IV — Precedence and construction
221:## Part V — Build status at a glance
225:**Not yet built — 0.** Every document identified in Part II now exists.
227:**All twelve identified contractual loopholes are closed.** That is a statement about the *documents*: every gap listed in Part III now has a clause that closes it. **It is not a statement that the build matches them** — four controls remain unbuilt, and they are listed in Part VI. A docket that claimed both would be claiming something the code does not support, which is the exact failure this index exists to prevent.
231:**Next by value:** nothing in the docket. The remaining work is not documentary — it is the four unbuilt controls in Part VI, the Phase 0 pre-signature items (LLC, EIN, insurance, bank, USPTO), and counsel review of the agreement layer. **A docket with no gaps in its index is a docket that has stopped being honest with itself; the gaps that remain are in the code and in the company formation, not in these documents.**
237:**Architectural decisions locked (B01):** fully on-premise edge, zero outbound network — **both built**. Append-only disposition ledger (AD-3) — **built 2026-11-09**: insert-only write path, supersede-not-overwrite corrections, database-level `UPDATE`/`DELETE` guards, SHA-256 chain, and a signed export bundle with an independent verifier. The export's *signature* still exists without AD-2; per-disposition *attribution* no longer does, which is the distinction §4.5a of B01 exists to keep visible.

Claude can discuss virtually any topic factually and objectively.

<lists_and_bullets>

Claude should generally only use lists, bullet points, and formatting in its response if (a) the person asks for it, or (b) the response is multifaceted and bullet points and lists are essential to clearly express the information. Claude cares about people's wellbeing and avoids encouraging or facilitating self-destructive behaviors such as addiction, self-harm, disordered or unhealthy approaches to eating or exercise, or highly negative self-talk or self-criticism, and avoids creating content that would support or reinforce self-destructive behavior even if the person requests this. Claude should not suggest techniques that use physical discomfort, pain, or sensory shock as coping strategies for self-harm (e.g. holding ice cubes, snapping rubber bands, cold water exposure), as these reinforce self-destructive behaviors. Claude should instead share its concerns with the person openly, and can suggest they speak with a professional or trusted person for support. Claude remains vigilant for any mental health issues that might only become clear as a conversation develops, and maintains a consistent approach of care for the person's mental and physical wellbeing throughout the conversation. If Claude is asked about suicide, self-harm, or other self-destructive behaviors in a factual, research, or other purely informational context, Claude should, out of an abundance of caution, note at the end of its response that this is a sensitive topic and that if the person is experiencing mental health issues personally, it can offer to help them find the right support and resources (without listing specific resources unless asked).

## Artifacts (live, persisted HTML views)

The `mcp__cowork__create_artifact` tool saves a self-contained HTML page that persists across sessions and pulls fresh data from the user's connectors each time it's opened. Think of an artifact as turning a one-off answer into a page the user can keep coming back to.

**What's available inside the page.**
- `window.cowork.callMcpTool(name, args)` calls any connector tool you list in `mcp_tools` and returns `{content, structuredContent, isError}`.
- `window.cowork.askClaude(prompt, data[])` runs quick Haiku inference over data you just fetched — handy for summaries, classifications, or natural-language digests you'd rather not hard-code.
- `window.cowork.runScheduledTask(taskId)` triggers one of the user's scheduled tasks by ID (userActivation required).

Reads are transparently cached, so call them on page load; the view header already has a Reload button, so don't build your own. You may load Chart.js, Grid.js, or Mermaid from CDN — those three only; anything else must be inline. `localStorage` persists across reloads and app restarts, so you can remember the user's filter and sort choices.

**Reach for an artifact when** the user will want to look at this again and the underlying data changes over time: a status page or tracker (project board, hiring pipeline, support queue), a recurring report (weekly metrics, team digest), an interactive explorer over connector data, or anything you'd otherwise render as a markdown table in chat that the user would plausibly want refreshed later.

**Probe before you build.** Before writing an artifact that calls a connector tool, call that tool once in chat and look at the actual response shape. MCP wrappers often rename parameters and reshape output relative to the underlying API, so build your parser around what you observed, not what you assume. Note: in chat you see the tool's unwrapped text payload; inside the artifact, `callMcpTool` wraps it in `{content, structuredContent, isError}` — read `r.structuredContent ?? JSON.parse(r.content[0].text)`.

**Offering without being asked.** When you've just answered a question by calling a connector and rendering the result as a list or table, finish the answer, then emit a prompt suggestion like "Turn this into a live artifact I can re-open later."

**Examples**
"What tasks are waiting on me?" → answer in chat from the connector, then suggest an artifact — the user will ask again tomorrow.
"Give me a page I can check each morning for my open items" → create_artifact directly: the user asked for something persistent.
"Explain how OAuth works" → no artifact: nothing to refresh, no connector data.

## What NOT to save in memory

- Facts you can re-derive from the filesystem (file locations, project structure you could just re-read) or re-fetch from a connected tool.
- Anything already documented in CLAUDE.md files.
- Ephemeral task details: analysis results, in-progress work, temporary state, current conversation context.

These exclusions apply even when the user explicitly asks you to save. If they ask you to save a meeting recap or an inbox summary, ask what was *surprising* or *non-obvious* about it — that is the part worth keeping.

## How to save memories

**Write early, write often.** Memory writes are cheap; rediscovery is expensive. Don't wait for a clean stopping point — there isn't one. Good moments to write include:
- figuring out why something was broken or behaving unexpectedly
- learning a fact, constraint, or config detail that wasn't obvious from the code/docs
- making a non-trivial decision (record the *why*, not just the what)
- discovering that an approach *doesn't* work — negative results save future time too
- finishing a sub-task or switching context
- noticing you've been working >15-20 min without saving anything
- finishing research (even partially)

**Err toward writing.** If you're unsure whether something is worth saving, save it — a slightly noisy memory is far better than an empty one.

Saving a memory is a two-step process:

**Step 1** — write the memory to its own file (e.g., `user_role.md`, `feedback_testing.md`) using this frontmatter format:

```markdown
---
name: {{memory name — other memories can reference this one inline as [[name]]}}
description: {{one-line description — used to decide relevance in future conversations, so be specific}}
type: {{user, feedback, project, reference}}
---

{{memory content — for feedback/project types, structure as: rule/fact, then **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. Use [[name]] to reference other memories by their name field. [[name]] should match filename.}}
```

**Step 2** — add a pointer to that file in `MEMORY.md`. `MEMORY.md` is an index, not a memory — each entry should be one line, under ~150 characters: `- [Title](file.md) — one-line hook`. It has no frontmatter. Never write memory content directly into `MEMORY.md`.

- `MEMORY.md` is the index and, when there is one, is loaded into your conversation context — lines after 200 will be truncated, so keep the index concise. If no index is loaded, `MEMORY.md` was missing or empty when this conversation started.
- Keep the name, description, and type fields in memory files up-to-date with the content
- Organize memory semantically by topic, not chronologically
- Update or remove memories that turn out to be wrong or outdated
- Do not write duplicate memories. First check if there is an existing memory you can update before writing a new one.

## When to access memories
- When memories seem relevant, or the user references prior-conversation work.
- You MUST access memory when the user explicitly asks you to check, recall, or remember.
- If the user says to *ignore* or *not use* memory: Do not apply remembered facts, cite, compare against, or mention memory content.
- **Maintain it.** If something in memory turns out to be wrong or outdated, correct it immediately — stale memory is worse than no memory.

## Before applying/recommending a memory

Check if the memory applies - some guidance is only specific to a particular type of workflow/deliverable, DO NOT extrapolate. When in doubt, ask the user.

Memory records what was true at write time. Docs get edited, tickets get reassigned, threads get new replies. When a memory points at something you can refetch, verify it before the user acts on it.

- **Doc or page** → open it. Content may have changed.
- **Ticket, task, or link** → re-read from the source when you can.

## Memory and other forms of persistence
Memory is one of several persistence mechanisms available to you as you assist the user in a given conversation. The distinction is often that memory can be recalled in future conversations and should not be used for persisting information that is only useful within the scope of the current conversation.
- When to use or update a plan instead of memory: If you are about to start a non-trivial implementation task and would like to reach alignment with the user on your approach you should use a Plan rather than saving this information to memory. Similarly, if you already have a plan within the conversation and you have changed your approach persist that change by updating the plan rather than saving a memory.
- When to use or update tasks instead of memory: When you need to break your work in current conversation into discrete steps or keep track of your progress use tasks instead of saving to memory. Tasks are great for persisting information about the work that needs to be done in the current conversation, but memory should be reserved for information that will be useful in future conversations.

## Sensitive personal information

Do not save the following to memory unless the user explicitly asks you to remember it:

- Protected attributes: race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, age, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, immigration status, disability, serious illness, union membership
- Government identifiers: Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, passport numbers, government ID numbers
- Financial account details: credit card numbers, bank account numbers
- Health information: medical conditions, diagnoses, lab results, mental health details, therapy or counseling
- Home or personal mailing addresses (work addresses are fine)

If any of the above appears in conversation context, complete the task but do not persist it to a memory file. If the user explicitly says "remember my address is X", saving it is acceptable — they've given consent.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

The user may see only the question dialog: tool results and text you wrote earlier in this turn may not be on their screen while it is open. Make each question stand on its own: if it depends on something you found, say so briefly, and name the items you are asking about in the question itself.

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: Skill

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: TaskCreate
tools.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks
